headline: Adopted FY27 commercial property tax shift at 1.03 and approved $132,000 Harbor Walk and $124,300 Railroad Ave housing grants.
summary: Engineers presented the plan for the wastewater treatment upgrade, with construction expected to finish by the end of 2030. The council also dropped a rule requiring city fee changes to be published in a local newspaper and withdrew a proposed lot-size change for coastal residential zoning. Councilors appointed Angela Sanfilippo to the Fisheries Commission.
decisions: Appointed Angela Sanfilippo to the Fisheries Commission, 9-0.
Referred a zoning amendment to P&D and the Planning Board, with a public hearing set for December 8, 2026, 9-0.
Approved a $389.76 budget transfer to cover a salary shortfall in Veterans Services, 9-0.
Accepted $65 in cash donations to the Archives Department, 9-0.
Accepted $3,720.01 in cash donations to Veterans Services, 9-0.
Accepted a $100 donation to the Community Impact Unit, 9-0.
Accepted a $124,300 state Housing Choice Grant for the Railroad Ave 40R project, 9-0.
Accepted a $132,000 state grant to refresh and strengthen the Harbor Walk, 8-1.
Accepted a donated framed portrait of former City Clerk Joanne M. Senos, valued at about $150, 8-0.
Withdrew a proposed change to the minimum lot area for RC-40 coastal residential zoning, 9-0.
Failed motion to set the commercial tax shift at 1.0 for FY27, 2-7.
Adopted a commercial tax shift of 1.03 for FY27, 8-1.
Amended the city code to remove the newspaper publishing requirement for fee changes, 8-0.

Bob Parsons stated the above was the timeline of construction.
Councilor Nolan asked when the odor control device was removed, would there be something installed in its
place to maintain odor control. Eric Kelley stated that during construction a temporary odor control that used
activated carbon would be installed and be used until the permanent part of the facility could be constructed. 
Councilor Benson asked why would construction take so long, and would costs go up during the extended
construction. Bob Parsons stated that it would take two years to prep the ground for the pouring of concrete to
make the process tanks, and then it would take a year and a half to install the equipment into the tanks. He stated
that once that portion of construction was completed, it would meet the State’s mandate for the project, and the
quality of the discharge into the Outer Harbor would be improved. He stated that there would then be a second
phase of construction to reconfigure the site. He stated that the project was being run under a construction
management at risk methodology as it would give the City better cost control. He stated that pricing would be
solicited and a hard cost of the project would be determined by January, which would lock in the maximum price
of the work. DPW Director, Michael Hale stated that four years for construction of a project this complex would
go by quickly. He stated that this was the largest construction project the City had undertaken. 
Councilor Page gave thanks to Senator Bruce Tarr for his work in securing the $5 million MassWorks grant for
the project. She asked for clarification on the piling field that was required for the project. Bob Parsons stated
that the pilings had to be driven to a certain depth to prevent the tanks from lifting from the ground and to support
the weight of the tanks when full. He stated that there would be hundreds of pilings put into the ground, and a
final number would be determined soon. 
Councilor Page asked what the cost of the piling field would be. Bob Parsons stated that the earthworks and the
deep foundation portion of the project was $33 million. 
Councilor Margiotta asked if the City could receive more grants in the future for the project. Michael Hale
stated that the City would continue to pursue grants, and any funding possible, but there were no large grants
available to significantly decrease costs. He stated there may be the possibility of some principal forgiveness on
the loan from the State as well. 
Councilor Memhard asked what the pilings were made of. Bob Parsons stated they were steel and would be
filled with concrete.

had been part of that bill. 
Councilor Benson asked what was being done to harden the site from cyber-attacks. Michael Hale stated that a
primary wastewater treatment plant wouldn’t be a primary target, but it was being looked at during construction.
Councilor Gross asked for clarification on how the Headworks building would be upgrade while maintaining
operations. Bob Parsons stated that bypasses would be arranged during construction.
Councilor Gross asked what would be built in place of the clarifiers. Bob Parsons stated that the permanent
odor control system would be in that location.

COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION: On a motion by Councilor Memhard, seconded by Councilor Page, the
Budget & Finance Committee voted 2 in favor, 1 opposed (Page), to recommend that the City Council accept
under MGL c. 44, §53A, a state grant from the Mass. Executive Office of Economic Development, Massachusetts
Downtown Initiative Capital Grant in the amount of $132,000 for the purpose of refreshing and strengthening the
Harbor Walk. There are no local matching requirements for the grant and the period is from January 1, 2027
through April 30, 2028.
Summary of Discussion: Councilor Page stated that the grant would pay for the instillation of wayfinding signs
around downtown. She stated that there would be thermoplastic sidewalk reflective tape for the Harbor Walk
which should be trialed on Rocky Neck before being used downtown. She stated that there would also be popcorn
signs, and the number and location of these was unknown at this time. She stated that anchor art instillations
would also be installed and those had not been vetted or decided yet. She stated that these were all concentrated
in a small quarter mile corridor and the scope should be expanded along Commercial Street and along Rogers
Street terminating at Pratty’s which would be inside the Designated Port Area. She stated that the there was a
lack of public process in the grant application process. 
Community Development Director, Alex Koppelman stated that this grant had been applied for by his
department and it aligned with the department’s goals. He stated that it had come from several planning processes
including the local Rapid Recovery Plan and the City’s Comprehensive Plan.
Economic Development Coordinator, Emily Sloane stated that the funds from this grant would be funding the
second phase of the wayfinding signage project. She stated that several large directory signs had recently been
installed, mostly on Rogers Street, and these were part of a larger wayfinding design package. She stated this
package included other types of signs and locations, and the next phase would include smaller directional signs,
another directory sign, and a district identifier sign. She stated that these signs would not be along the waterfront,
but would in locations to direct visitors from the train station or Washington Street to the downtown area. She
stated the grant would also fund improving and enhancing the harbor walk in two key ways, by replacing the
existing worn-out signage on granite pillars, and secondly responding to community feedback to improve the
ability to follow the Harbor Walk by installing thermoplastic markers on the sidewalk. She stated that the markers
would last longer than painting a line to follower, and be less labor intensive then installing a brick line through
the Harbor Walk. She stated that these thermoplastic markers would only be installed in key locations where it
was not clear where the Harbor Walk went. She stated that there would be a community engagement process for
the design and location of these markers. 
Councilor Grace asked if the granite posts would be removed or just the signs replaced.  Emily Sloane stated
that only the signs would be replaced. 
Councilor Grace asked if there would be community engagement through the process of using these funds.
Emily Sloane stated that there would be community engagement with waterfront stakeholders.
Councilor Grace asked for clarification of what a thermoplastic marker was. Emily Sloane stated that it was a
two-dimensional piece of art that would be affixed to the sidewalk, but the design had not been decided. She
stated they were meant to make the Harbor Walk easier to navigate.
City Council                                         October 27, 2026                                                  Page 12 of 22
Councilor Grace stated that the grant did not determine the location or design of any of the signage.
Councilor Page stated that she had received conflicting information regarding the signs that had been installed
so far and the cost.
Councilor Benson asked if the signs at all 42 granite posts would be replaced. Emily Sloane stated that there
were at least two signs per post, and some were outdated, but all signs would be replaced with relevant content. 
Councilor Grow asked if the signs that were being replaced would impede business on the waterfront. Emily
Sloane stated they would not.
Councilor Page stated that the thermoplastic markers may be raised and impact traffic.
Councilor Nolan asked if the QR codes on the Harbor Walk were currently functional. Emily Sloane stated that
Miranda Aisling Hynes had taken an inventory and any that were not functional had been updated by IT.
Councilor Gross stated that it was unfortunate that the directory signs had been designed in a “north up”
orientation rather than site specific orientation. He stated that having better wayfinding, such as to parking areas
for visitors, was important. 
Councilor Page stated that she objected to the placement of the directory sign on the boulevard.
Councilor Grace stated that previously crosswalks in the City had been plastic that were slippery in the rain, so
the City should be cautious when designing the thermoplastic markers.
